title: Ki Tavo: first fruits (Deuteronomy 26:1–11)
hookLine: the farmer brings the first fruits in a basket and tells his people's story

lines: A FIG WITH A REED TIED ON.
A BASKET ON THE ROAD UP.
A FLUTE, AN OX, A VILLAGE.
cards: A farmer in the hills walks into his field early in the season and sees it: the first fig of the year, swelling on the branch. He doesn't eat it. He ties a reed around it, a little marker: this one is set aside.
Weeks later he carries it, with the first barley and grapes and olives, in a basket, up the road to Jerusalem.
The Mishnah describes the procession: an ox with gilded horns, a flute playing in front, whole villages walking together. And when he arrives, he has a speech to make.

teach.h: BIKKURIM: THE FIRST OF THE FRUIT.
teach.b: The word is bikkurim, first fruits, from the same Hebrew root as bechor, firstborn. The instruction in Deuteronomy twenty-six is simple.
When you come into the land and settle it, take some of the first of every fruit, put it in a basket, bring it to the place God chooses, and hand it to the priest.
Later tradition limited the offering to the seven kinds the land is praised for: wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives and dates. But the surprise isn't the fruit. It's the speech.
The farmer doesn't say, look what I grew. He tells history: a wandering ancestor, slavery in Egypt, a cry, a rescue, a land. Only then does he set the basket down.

The Mishnah adds a detail that's easy to miss. At first, people who could read the Hebrew recited it themselves, and those who couldn't were prompted. The ones who needed help were embarrassed, and some stopped coming.
So the rule changed: the priest read it for everyone, and everyone repeated after him, the scholar and the farmer who never learned to read, the same words at the same pace.

And the passage ends with joy: rejoice in all the good you've been given, you and your household, the Levite, and the stranger in your midst. The first doesn't go into storage, or straight into your own mouth.
It goes to thanks, and the thanks is shared.

how: Bikkurim were brought to the Temple between Shavuot and Sukkot. They have not been brought since the Temple's destruction, but verses from the farmer's declaration in Deuteronomy 26 (26:5–8) are expounded line by line in the Passover Haggadah, and Shavuot is still called the festival of first fruits.

firstborn sons, set aside at birth
first fruits, carried up in a basket

games.q: inside the basket — tap the pairs.

s: any fruit at all could be brought as bikkurim
tradition limited them to the land's seven kinds.
the farmer recited a history, not a list of his crops
a wandering ancestor, Egypt, rescue, then the land.
the rule changed so that people who couldn't read wouldn't be embarrassed
Mishnah Bikkurim 3:7: everyone repeats after the priest.

games.q: you've brought your first basket. some neighbors can't read the Hebrew declaration, and out of embarrassment they've stopped coming. what does the Mishnah say was done?
o: only those who can read may bring fruit.
the priest reads, and everyone repeats after him.
games.why: the rule changed for everyone, so the farmer who couldn't read stood exactly level with the scholar.

practice: Think about what comes first in your day: the first cup of coffee, the first hour, the first money of the month. Pick one, and before it's yours, imagine tying a reed around it: this one is marked.
Let the first sip, or the first quiet minute, carry a moment of thanks.
